transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-05T16:00:00Z
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Arjun Patel (Redwood SE), Sofia Ruiz (Redwood SE), Daniel Park (Polaris ML), Lena Ortiz (Polaris PM), Rajiv Menon (Polaris SRE), Tasha Nguyen (Polaris Regulatory)

Summary:
A scoping session to finalize the POC quality evaluation plan: define golden prompts, regression tests, hallucination and format checks, scoring approach and load/bench timings. Customer prioritized correctness/format over lowest cost but wants latency SLOs.

Topics covered:
- Success criteria and weighting (accuracy, hallucination rate, format compliance, latency, cost)
- Golden prompt set composition and seeding strategy
- Regression test harness and CI gating rules
- Hallucination detection heuristics and patching strategy
- Benchmark load profile (QPS, tokens per request, concurrency) and timeline
- Data privacy, SOC2/SSO, private vs hosted concerns

Action items (discussed): see metadata field.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): OK, hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick roll call?
[00:10] Daniel (Polaris): hi all, Daniel here — head of ML. Lena and Rajiv are with me as well.
[00:14] Lena (Polaris PM): hi, yeah thanks, excited to get this scoped.
[00:17] Arjun (Redwood SE): great, i'll jump into the technical goals after Maya quickly frames the business objectives.
[00:22] Maya: perfect. Polaris told us earlier that the POC success criteria are mostly quality focused — accuracy, low hallucination, and strict response formatting for downstream parsers. cost and latency are secondary but still important. is that right?
[00:36] Daniel: yes that's the short version. we want the model to produce a structured JSON snippet for 95% of queries with less than 3% hallucination on named entities in the finance domain. latency target is 300–500 ms p50 for typical queries.
[00:50] Rajiv: and from infra, we need to validate sustained 40 qps with burst to 120 for 30s windows, so the benchmark plan needs to include load shape.
[01:02] Arjun: ok noted. for the quality eval itself we usually split into automated metrics and human review. automated checks cover schema/format, exact-match fields, fuzzy entity match for named entities, and a hallucination detector; human review covers edge cases and ambiguous prompts.
[01:18] Lena: when you say hallucination detector, is that a heuristic checks, or model-based? how do you measure it?
[01:24] Arjun: good question. we use a mixed approach: rule-based checks (e.g., verifying entities against a provided canonical list), embedding-similarity checks for factual claims against a small knowledge base, and optionally a secondary verification model that flags probable hallucinations. for the POC we can start with rule-based + embedding threshold, then add the verifier if needed.
[01:42] Tasha (Regulatory): will you need any raw customer data to run that? from a compliance perspective we need logs redacted and no PII leaving the VPC if we go private.
[01:50] Sofia (Redwood): we can run both hosted and private sims. for hosted we ask for anonymized examples only, and we keep logs per our SOC2 practices — we'll send the security FAQ.
[01:58] Daniel: ok we'll anonymize, but we also want to test realistic failure modes so we might provide synthetic records for edge cases.
[02:04] Arjun: perfect. partition the dataset into: golden set (200 examples), regression set (1,800 examples), and holdout (200) for final verification — that's a typical split we recommend.
[02:16] Lena: 200 golden seems small; how do you ensure it covers domain variety?
[02:20] Arjun: golden should be curated: 50 canonical positive templates, 30 tricky edge cases, 60 entity-heavy financial tasks, 30 formatting/escape cases, 30 adversarial hallucination examples. we seed golden from your top-traffic intents and historical failures.
[02:33] Daniel: sounds reasonable. for scoring, we want a single composite score to decide pass/fail for the POC, but also component metrics. can you propose a weighting?
[02:40] Maya: typical starting weighting we use is accuracy/format 50%, hallucination penalty 30%, latency/cost 20% combined, with thresholds that must be met for pass. but we can tweak per customer.
[02:50] Lena: we want format compliance to be hard fail: if JSON schema isn't followed, downstream systems break. so even if the score is high, any format schema failure should be a showstopper for that example.
[02:59] Arjun: agree. we'll implement hard gating on schema checks: examples failing schema get flagged and excluded from automated composite score but counted as failures in the report.
[03:09] Rajiv: on hallucination measurement — you mentioned entity canonical lists. we can provide a names/identifier corpus for Polaris securities, tickers, and bank names. would that be sufficient?
[03:19] Arjun: yes, that materially helps. embedding-based checks will compare response claims to the KB and if similarity below threshold we flag it. we'll provide false positive/negative calibration guidance.
[03:29] Daniel: what's a realistic hallucination threshold? 3% across the regression set?
[03:34] Arjun: 3% is aggressive but feasible; depends on prompt engineering and model variant. for early baseline we aim for <=6% then optimize.
[03:41] Lena: ok timeline — how long do you need to run a proper regression?
[03:45] Maya: typical run is one week for initial baseline (hosted) including prompt tuning and one dedicated config run (if you choose Dedicated) the following week for throughput/latency. so about two weeks end-to-end for initial pass.
[03:56] Daniel: do you need a canary or warmup before the dedicated run?
[03:59] Arjun: yes, we'll do warmup sequences and KV cache priming for a 2 hour window and ramp tests for concurrency.
[04:06] Tasha: can you describe what info you capture in logs? i.e., are outputs stored, and how long?
[04:11] Sofia: we'll capture request/response, model id, latency, and scoring signals for the eval; retention policy can be set per agreement. for hosted we retain minimal logs for 30 days by default; for private deployments we follow your retention policy.
[04:24] Daniel: great. on the scoring side, what automated metrics do you produce?
[04:28] Arjun: we produce exact match %, schema pass %, normalized entity F1, embedding-distance hallucination rate, and a cost-per-request metric. we also produce human-review adjustment factors.
[04:38] Lena: do you do BLEU/ROUGE etc? is that useful for us?
[04:42] Arjun: for generative templates BLEU/ROUGE add little value; we prefer exact-match or token-level normalized edit distance for structured outputs. for free-text responses we can compute ROUGE but we'll prioritize human judgments.
[04:55] Daniel: i want to see an example rubric for human review — like severity levels for hallucination and how they map to pass/fail.
[05:01] Maya: we'll include a suggested 3-tier severity: minor (formatting/typo but no factual error), major (incorrect entity values that could cause downstream misprocessing), and critical (materially wrong financial claim). major+critical count as failures in the composite.
[05:15] Lena: ok. regarding golden prompts — who curates them? we expect collaboration.
[05:20] Arjun: Redwood will provide a first-draft golden set curated from your top intents; you review and augment. We iterate until both parties sign off.
[05:28] Rajiv: about the load profile— 40 qps sustained, 120 burst — what hardware footprint do you simulate for dedicated?
[05:34] Arjun: depends on model size and quantization. rough rule: a 7B quantized model can hit that qps on a 2-GPU pool with batching; 13B requires 4 GPUs. we'll propose a baseline config and cost estimate in the bench spreadsheet.
[05:47] Tasha: any privacy concerns for sending the 2k prompts?
[05:50] Maya: redact PII; we also accept synthetic equivalents. if you prefer, we can run on your private deployment image so data never leaves your VPC.
[05:59] Daniel: let's try hosted baseline with anonymized data first, then private if we need on-prem keys.
[06:03] Lena: timeline recap?
[06:05] Maya: plan: Redwood sends draft golden prompts + rubric by 8/10, Polaris provides datasets by 8/12, baseline hosted run week of 8/17, dedicated sim (if requested) week of 8/24, and final report by 8/28.
[06:16] Daniel: that timeline works.
[06:18] Arjun: one more technical note — hallucination detector thresholds will be tuned on your holdout set; we'll share calibration notes and false-positive rate targets.
[06:27] Lena: how will we consume results? dashboard, CSV?
[06:30] Sofia: both. Redwood Console export includes per-example results, summary dashboards, and a regression CSV that you can plug into your CI. we'll share a sample export format.
[06:39] Rajiv: for CI gating, can we set a nightly regression check that fails the build if composite drops 5%?
[06:44] Arjun: yes, we can integrate with your CI (we've done Jenkins/GitLab/GitHub actions hooks) to post pass/fail. we'll document the webhook and payload.
[06:53] Tasha: send over SOC2 cert and SAML SSO setup docs.
[06:56] Maya: will do — action item.
[06:58] Lena: ok thanks everyone, seems actionable.
[07:02] Maya: thanks, i'll follow up with the plan and spreadsheets. bye.

End of transcript.
